https://www.cei.int/ansa/178219.text: Europe's Tallest Statue of the Virgin Mary Soars Above the Skies of Poland (ANSA) - KONOTOPIE, 25 LUG - In a village in central Poland, a statue of the Virgin Mary soars above the fleecy July skies: while churches are emptying in this country with a long Catholic tradition, a tycoon has had Europe's tallest Marian monument erected there. Rising to a height of 55 meters, the white silhouette of concrete and steel beams stands, rigid and solemn, amid a sea of greenery and parking lots in the rural town of Konotopie, a three-hour drive northwest of Warsaw. Its dedication and blessing are scheduled for the Feast of the Assumption, August 15. For now, construction is still in full swing, under the dazed or fervent gaze of visitors. The Poles owe this gift to a multimillionaire compatriot, Roman Karkosik, who has spent some 100 million zlotys (23.1 million euros), according to local media. He himself lives nearby, in the neighboring town of Kikol, in a restored 18th-century palace across from the parish church. - Funding Devotion - For the faithful interviewed by AFP, devotion is priceless. "People come here (...) in search of faith," says Marek Gizinski, who traveled dozens of kilometers to pray. "And as with any miracle (...) you simply can't forget it—it's downright impossible to forget," he whispers, his gaze fixed on the Virgin Mary. Some local residents, however, believe that this giant statue is not the best way to represent the Catholic faith in a country already dotted with religious monuments, many of which commemorate the Polish Pope John Paul II. The country's main site of Marian devotion—a painting known as the "Black Madonna," located in the south—attracts between 3.5 and 5 million pilgrims each year. "Rather than for the Virgin, that money 'should have been invested in a hospital or an orphanage,'" laments a couple who came from the neighborhood. Entrepreneur Karkosik and his wife, among the wealthiest people in Poland, recently came to admire their creation—in a luxury car with a chauffeur. "Last Sunday, he came to visit the construction site from the back seat of his Maybach," jokes Andrzej, the site's caretaker. - A New Pilgrimage Site? - Local officials hope the project will bring economic benefits—unanticipated in this impoverished region. "I haven't heard any negative opinions (...) Everyone is generally satisfied," Renata Golebiewska, mayor of the neighboring town of Kikol, told AFP. In 2024, municipal tax revenue per capita in Kikol amounted to just 1,117 zlotys (258 euros), according to data from the Ministry of Finance—making it one of the least well-funded municipalities in the region. The statue in Konotopie is the second-tallest in the world after the "Mother of All Asia—Tower of Peace," completed in 2021 and standing 98.15 meters tall in Batangas City, Philippines, another deeply Catholic country. The Virgin Mary holds a special place in Poland's religious and national identity, where she has been venerated for centuries as the country's patroness and protector—even as the country experiences one of the fastest rates of secularization in the world. "We hope that this place will bear the fruits of a deeper return to the faith, or at least help people deepen their faith," says the parish priest, Marek Mrowczynski. Not entirely convinced, Wanda, who came with two friends, wonders above all how much the developers "are going to pocket." kw/ks/pop/jrt (ANSA). https://english.elpais.com/international.text: The fact that Spain is swimming against the tide on European immigration issues became more evident than ever on Friday, when several EU leaders led by the prime ministers of Denmark and Italy — Mette Frederiksen and Giorgia Meloni — strongly criticized the Spanish government’s decision earlier this year to grant legal status to potentially hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants. One of the toughest statements came from Frederiksen, who despite being one of the few social-democratic leaders in Europe, has opposing views to Spain’s socialist leader Pedro Sánchez when it comes to immigration. The Danish prime minister accused Sánchez of doing “almost the exact opposite” of what other EU member states are doing on this matter, and asked the European Commission, the union’s executive arm, to scrutinize Spain’s position. “I have asked the European Commission to examine what happens when a country does almost the exact opposite of what the rest of us are doing,” she said. “I believe this runs counter to the migration policy supported by a large majority in Europe today.” Frederiksen’s statements came after the by now traditional “migration breakfast” bringing together 18 member states as well as the European Commission, with a view to further restrict common immigration policies, among other things by accelerating the creation of third-country deportation centers. The Czech Republic’s prime minister, Andrej Babis, was also openly critical of Spain’s policy. “We see what is happening in Spain, how some politicians are capable of population replacement just to stay in their jobs and in government,” he said as he walked into the summit. And the Austrian chancellor, Christian Stocker, said it was a “bad sign” for Europe. According to diplomatic sources, several participants declared their intention to revisit the final conclusions of the document that will emerge from the summit in order to underscore their rejection of Spain’s plan to legalize undocumented migrants, which they see as having a “pull effect.” Many see evidence of this in the crisis experienced in Ceuta, a Spanish exclave city in northern Africa whose borders were stormed by around 80,000 people in just two days in late July. The city has yet to recover from the effects of the sudden influx, and thousands of migrants remain in makeshift camps and reception centers. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen noted in a letter before the summit that Europe’s policies are already achieving “substantial results,” including a 55% drop in illegal border crossings in the last two years, down to their lowest level since 2021. One source said ahead of the summit that even though the facts do not support the popular idea of uncontrolled immigration in Europe, “some countries are looking for a more emotional debate because they need it for domestic reasons,” citing a series of general elections coming up — beginning with Spain, which has called a snap election on November 29, to be followed by elections in France, Finland and others next year. Diplomatic sources said that the initiative to introduce amendments to the final conclusions — which must be adopted by consensus, which means Spain could block that section of it — was led by Denmark, Italy and Poland. The changes would involve underscoring that illegal immigration is something of concern to EU citizens, and that more work needs to be done to “reduce” the pull effect and any policies that might incentivize immigration to Europe. Those countries also want to explore ways to “encourage cooperation” among member states “when they enact national policies that affect others,” alluding once again to Spain’s plan to legalize migrants, which they feel could impact their own countries.
